blocks.text: Retrieval fine-tuning trains a model to find the most relevant documents for a given query from a large collection, extending the embeddings and vector search concepts covered in the earlier RAG and Vector Search course into a specific fine-tuning task.

This topic covers how retrieval training data is structured around positive and negative pairs, the difference between bi-encoder and cross-encoder architectures, and the retrieval-specific evaluation metrics that matter here.
1. What Retrieval Fine-Tuning Targets

blocks.alt: A query goes through a fine-tuned retrieval model, producing relevant documents

blocks.text: Retrieval fine-tuning teaches a model to score or rank documents by relevance to a given query, more reliably surfacing the most useful documents from a large collection than an off-the-shelf general purpose embedding model, covered in the earlier RAG course, might manage alone.
2. General Purpose vs Domain-Tuned Retrieval

blocks.alt: General purpose embeddings are compared against domain tuned retrieval

blocks.text: A general purpose embedding model captures broad semantic similarity reasonably well, fine-tuning on domain-specific query and document pairs, legal search, medical literature, internal company documentation, sharpens retrieval accuracy specifically for that domain vocabulary and relevance notion.
3. Positive and Negative Training Pairs

blocks.alt: A query with a relevant document and a query with an irrelevant document form a contrastive training pair

blocks.text: Retrieval training data is built from contrastive pairs, a query paired with a genuinely relevant document as a positive example, and a query paired with an irrelevant document as a negative example, the model learns to score positive pairs higher than negative ones.
4. Random Negatives vs Hard Negatives

blocks.alt: Random negatives are compared against hard negatives that are similar but wrong

blocks.text: Random negatives, documents unrelated to the query in any obvious way, are easy for a model to distinguish from the true positive, hard negatives, documents that are topically similar but still not the correct answer, force the model to learn a much finer grained notion of relevance, generally producing a stronger retrieval model.

blocks.text: 5. Bi-Encoder vs Cross-Encoder Architectures

blocks.alt: A bi-encoder embeds query and document separately while a cross-encoder scores them jointly

blocks.text: A bi-encoder embeds the query and each document separately, then compares embeddings, covered in the earlier RAG course, fast enough to search a large collection efficiently, a cross-encoder instead processes the query and a candidate document together, jointly, producing a more accurate but much more computationally expensive relevance score, a tradeoff that shapes how each is used in practice.

blocks.title: This tradeoff explains why retrieval and re-ranking are often separate stages
blocks.content: A fast bi-encoder retrieval fine-tuning pass narrows a large collection down to a manageable candidate set, then a more expensive cross-encoder re-ranking pass, covered in the next topic, refines the final ranking among just those candidates.

blocks.text: 6. Retrieval Fine-Tuning vs Re-Ranker Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: Retrieval fine-tuning is distinct from re-ranker fine-tuning, covered in the next topic

blocks.text: Retrieval fine-tuning as covered here typically trains the bi-encoder stage that efficiently narrows a large collection to a candidate set, re-ranker fine-tuning, covered in the next topic, trains the more precise but more expensive stage that refines ranking among that smaller candidate set, the two stages commonly work together in a full retrieval pipeline.
7. Retrieval-Specific Evaluation Metrics

blocks.alt: Recall at K, MRR, and NDCG are retrieval specific evaluation metrics

blocks.text: Retrieval evaluation uses metrics distinct from the classification metrics covered earlier in this module, recall at K measuring whether a relevant document appears within the top K results, mean reciprocal rank rewarding relevant results appearing earlier, and NDCG accounting for graded relevance rather than simple binary relevant or not.
8. Building a Retrieval Fine-Tuning Dataset

Retrieval training data commonly comes from historical search logs, where a clicked or engaged-with result serves as an implicit positive signal, combined with deliberately mined hard negatives, similar documents that were shown but not selected, a practical data source distinct from purely manually annotated data.
9. Common Production Use Cases

Retrieval fine-tuning commonly powers enterprise search, customer support knowledge base lookup, and the retrieval stage of a retrieval augmented generation pipeline, covered in the earlier RAG course, cases where finding the right small set of relevant documents from a much larger collection is the critical first step.
Worked Example

A company building an internal knowledge base search fine-tunes a bi-encoder retrieval model on query and document pairs mined from their search logs, initially using only random negatives sampled from unrelated documents.

Evaluation using recall at K shows decent but not great performance, switching to hard negatives, documents that share vocabulary with the query but are not actually the correct answer, and retraining meaningfully improves recall at K, since the model now learns finer distinctions than random negatives alone could teach.
Common Mistakes

items: Training only on random negatives, missing the sharper relevance signal hard negatives provide
Using a cross-encoder architecture for first-stage retrieval over a large collection, where its computational cost is impractical
Evaluating retrieval quality with classification metrics instead of recall at K, MRR, or NDCG
Treating retrieval fine-tuning and re-ranker fine-tuning as interchangeable rather than complementary pipeline stages

blocks.text: Practice

For a search or retrieval task you are familiar with, write one query, one positive document, one random negative document, and one hard negative document that is topically similar but still wrong, then explain why the hard negative would be more useful for training than the random one.
Key Takeaway

Retrieval fine-tuning trains a bi-encoder model on contrastive query and document pairs, with hard negatives producing sharper relevance learning than random negatives, evaluated using recall at K, MRR, and NDCG rather than classification metrics, and it typically forms the first, efficient stage of a pipeline that the re-ranker fine-tuning covered in the next topic refines further.
